paras: The killing of Jerry Hamilton was the fatal beating of a Black plantation worker by masked men near Red Bluff, Montgomery County, Georgia, on the night of May 2, 1881. A mass meeting at Mount Vernon denounced it, and in June ten local men were brought to Savannah on a federal civil rights warrant.
Hamilton, "a colored man," worked on Asa Adams's plantation; a Red Bluff correspondent of the Eastman Times called him "a peaceable, hardworking negro" with a large family.

On the night of Monday, May 2, a party of masked men took Hamilton from his house, carried him about a quarter of a mile away, beat and stamped him, and apparently threw him into a branch. His wife found him the next morning on a log, partly in the water, and he died that day, reportedly after naming several of the party, whom he knew only by their voices.

The correspondent had heard nothing of an inquest verdict, and none appears in the coverage. According to the South Georgian, as quoted, white and colored citizens met at Mount Vernon on May 10 and adopted resolutions denouncing the crime and offering relief to the family.

United States Commissioner Wade later issued a warrant charging Montgomery County men with violating the civil rights law, and a deputy marshal brought them to Savannah on June 14. The paper counted ten but named nine, among them Joseph Palmer, William Adams, and Thomas and Angus Norris; they gave bond, and no report of the examination set for the next day was found.

Both items ran in the Savannah Morning News. On May 16 it reprinted the Eastman Times letter, which called the killing an "awful deed" and urged "the extreme punishment" for all concerned. Its June 15 report, headlined "A Cowardly Crime. Ten Respectable Citizens Charged With a Serious Offense," condemned the killing but called the accused "among the most prominent and worthy citizens of Montgomery," against whom there appeared to be "no evidence."

The South Georgian dated the mass meeting May 10, while the June Savannah report placed it the day after the killing. The correspondent wrote that no cause was assigned, whereas the Savannah paper said Hamilton had "in some manner" made himself "obnoxious."

reader.title: Killing of Jerry Hamilton
bases: A party of masked or disguised men took Hamilton from his house at night and beat him to death (A2, A3).

A masked party, of which Hamilton reportedly named 'several', took him from his home and beat him fatally without any lawful authority (A2, A3); the Red Bluff correspondent said no cause was assigned, while the Savannah paper said only that he had 'rendered himself obnoxious', so the pretext is not established (A2, A3).

The Eastman Times correspondent's letter (A2) and the Savannah paper's own report of the arrests (A3), drawn from different sources, agree that disguised men took Hamilton from his house on the night of May 2 and beat him to death.

accounts.label: Red Bluff correspondent (Eastman Times)
accounts.gist: Masked men took Hamilton from his house, beat and stamped him, and apparently left him for dead in a branch; he died the next day after naming several attackers to his wife; no cause was known.

accounts.label: Savannah Morning News local report
accounts.gist: Disguised men beat to death a Black man who had 'in some manner' made himself obnoxious; the ten men arrested federally were respectable citizens against whom there appeared to be no evidence.

framing.detail: The Eastman Times correspondent, reprinted in Savannah briefs, called it an 'awful deed' and 'sickening outrages' and urged 'the extreme punishment' for all concerned.
Headlined 'A Cowardly Crime. Ten Respectable Citizens Charged With a Serious Offense', the Savannah report condemned the killing but defended the accused and disputed federal jurisdiction.
